title: Understanding the marketplace & trends
source: Session 3 handout (DDM 26/27) – Mason et al. (2015) Trend Driven Innovation, Raymond (2019), Buzasi et al. (2017), Euromonitor snack-market activity
tagline: Marketing insights come from looking back (market data), at the present (real-time tracking) and forward (trends). Secondary research and databases describe the market; the Consumer Trend Canvas turns a trend into an innovation.
goals: define **marketing insights** and distinguish them from market research
compare **primary and secondary research** and name the key sections of a **market analysis**
define a **consumer trend** and distinguish **micro vs. macro** trends
explain **weak signals, cultural brailling and horizon scanning**
fill in the **Consumer Trend Canvas** (basic needs, drivers of change, emerging expectations, inspirations → apply)

items.text: The capacity to gain an accurate and deep understanding of someone or something (Oxford) – a clear, deep and sometimes sudden understanding of a complicated problem (Cambridge).

Knowledge and understanding about a market, its consumers and the companies operating in it – generated by observing consumer, company and stakeholder behaviour (data collection and analysis of behaviours, lifestyles, markets and cultures).

blocks.title: Insights unlock opportunities by …
items: providing a deeper understanding of consumer behaviour and its drivers
tracking changes in consumer needs and desires
understanding how different consumer groups perceive the world and culture around them

steps.label: Looking back
steps.text: Past behaviour, consumption patterns, historical market data, statistics and trends

steps.label: Real time
steps.text: Track behaviour now – Voice of Customer, NPS

steps.label: Looking forward
steps.text: Predict behaviour via trend forecasting and statistical modelling

blocks.title: Marketing research ≠ marketing insights
blocks.text: Discovery > insights: market research is only **one of the tools** for discovery. Insights are fundamental to understand a marketplace and identify emerging trends.

sides.label: Primary research
points: By the company itself or a market research firm
Experimental vs. non-experimental
Qualitative vs. quantitative
Tailored, but expensive and slow

sides.label: Secondary research
points: Internal (company records) vs. external (databases, reports)
Usually more **time- and cost-effective**
Focus of this session

blocks.title: Marketing research process (5 steps)

steps.label: 1 · Problem
steps.text: Formulate the research problem or question

steps.label: 2 · Design
steps.text: Determine information sources and research design

blocks.note: Steps 2 and 3 decide on the types of data and the methods required to collect them.

sections.heading: Market analysis with secondary data
sections.lead: A market analysis is a quantitative and qualitative assessment of a market: size in volume and value, segments, lifestyles and buying patterns, competition, environment, barriers to entry and regulation.

items.label: Industry description & outlook
items.text: Current state and forecasts: market size, trends, life cycle, projected growth, segmentation

items.label: Target market
items.text: Segments by demographics, psychographics, needs, purchase behaviour, emerging expectations – quantified in size and value

items.label: Competitive analysis
items.text: Competitors' positioning, strengths and weaknesses, marketing and distribution strategies

items.label: Distribution channels
items.text: Existing and emerging channels, connection to customers, channel power, role of online

items.label: Barriers to entry
items.text: Pitfalls and cost of entering – your potential weaknesses in this market

items.label: Regulation
items.text: Government rules and restrictions – estimate your compliance costs

blocks.title: Databases (ESCP library)
head: Database
What you find
rows: International market analyses, statistics on consumers, countries and companies (used for the Mexico/Japan snack-market activity)
Insights platform on new consumer behaviour and industry trends
Statistics portal: market studies, forecasts, consumer studies, demographics, polls
Industry studies and market analyses for French and international markets

items.text: The direction in which something tends to move and which has consequential impact on the culture, society or business environment through which it moves – not merely fashion; can be emotional, intellectual or spiritual.
A **new manifestation** among people – in behaviour, attitude or expectation – of a **fundamental human need, want or desire**.

sides.label: Micro trend
points: From early influencers to mass adoption in **1–2 years**
Important e.g. for fashion companies
Smaller-scale realisations of the desires behind macro trends

sides.label: Macro trend
points: Spans **at least 5 years**
Impacts many industries, from technology to finance
e.g. maker movement, wellness boom; evolves season to season on a continuum

blocks.title: The fundamental trend elements (Mason et al., 2015)

steps.label: Basic needs
steps.text: Fundamental, rarely changing human needs, wants and desires – central to spotting any trend

steps.label: Drivers of change
steps.text: No trend without change – analysing change is the core of forecasting

steps.label: Innovations
steps.text: Not trends themselves, but **examples** of how a trend exists; on-trend innovations hit the sweet spot

sections.heading: Identifying and evaluating trends
sections.lead: Forecasters look for patterns, weak signals, anomalies and disruptions at their earliest stage – watching innovators and early adopters for tension between what people want and what is available (Raymond, 2019).

items.label: Weak signal
items.text: An anomaly overlooked by mainstream organisations because it seems vague, random, disconnected, even surreal – meaningful once **organised in clusters across industries**.

items.label: Cultural brailling
items.text: Faith Popcorn's term: sampling and sensing change every day – feeling, smelling, tasting, experiencing shifts and anomalies.

items.label: Horizon scanning
items.text: The more **organised, structured** approach: scan the social, technological, economic, environmental, political, legal and ethical landscape (**STEEPLE**).

blocks.title: Horizon scanning – rule-of-thumb questions
items: Are the weak signals new, innovative, game-changing – and have early adopters started championing them?
Do they suggest a wider, deeper cultural shift, across key sectors (retail, fashion, travel, food, hospitality)?
Are they **memetic** – simple, easy to replicate, explain and visualise?
What friction or inflection points must they overcome; will the early or late majority resist?

blocks.title: Evaluating a trend for opportunity (Mattin et al., 2015)

items.label: Maturity
items.text: How are the expectations behind the trend playing out **now**? Adoption is fluid – Rogers' diffusion curve may be unreliable today.

items.label: Industry
items.text: How do the expectations play out in **my industry**? Learn from examples in other industries.

items.label: Locality
items.text: How do they play out in **my target market**? A trend must be adapted to the local context.

sections.heading: The Consumer Trend Canvas
sections.lead: A framework to unpack a trend and turn insights into an idea, product, service or other innovation. Work left (Analyse) to right (Apply), then summarise your idea.

sides.label: ANALYSE – unpack the trend
points: Basic needs: what deep consumer needs and desires does the trend address?

Drivers of change: why now? **Shifts** = long-term macro changes over years/decades (ageing society, urbanisation, climate challenge, rich–poor divide, people on the move, rising middle class); **triggers** = immediate changes (technologies, political/social events, economic shocks, environmental incidents)
Emerging expectations: new needs, wants and expectations created by the change – look for **expectation gaps**; new expectations are often set outside your industry
Inspirations: how are other businesses applying the trend? Look across industries, regions, cultures and firm types

sides.label: APPLY – use the trend
points: Innovation potential: where could you apply it? **Vision** (long-term direction), **business model** (new venture or brand), **product/service/experience**, **marketing** & communication
Who: which (new) customer groups? Think beyond demographics – needs, desires, expectations; use **personas** (a rich description of one fictional person representing a group)
Finally: summarise and describe your innovation idea

blocks.title: Mock exam: the Betterverse trend (LSN Global, 2022)
given: The metaverse as a new digital frontier; Gartner: by 2026 a quarter of people spend ≥ 1 h a day in it
57 % believe it can help address social problems created by the pandemic
Space for activism, aid, support, democratised access to services; low-impact interfaces, moral commerce
blocks.question: Classify: drivers of change, emerging expectations, basic needs.
steps: Drivers of change (why now?): **virtual lives**, **digital wellbeing** – not globalisation or ageing population
Emerging expectations (new demands): **increased inclusivity**, **democratisation of services**
Basic needs (timeless): **self-enhancement**, **inclusivity** (belonging) – convenience/personalisation are not the core here
blocks.result: Suggested solution (no official key). Test for each option: a change happening now (driver), a new demand on brands (expectation) or a timeless human need (basic need)?

blocks.title: Beneficial Intelligence (class activity)
blocks.text: Don't view the world through technology – view technology through **basic human needs**: “Save me time! Save me money! Make me a better person! Make everything easier!” Humans have limits, their expectations do not.

recap: Marketing insights = deep understanding of market, consumers and firms; research is only one discovery tool.
Insights look **back** (historical data), at the **present** (real-time, NPS) and **forward** (trend forecasting).
Secondary data is cheaper and faster; a market analysis covers industry outlook, target market, competition, channels, barriers to entry, regulation.
Consumer trend = new manifestation of a fundamental human need; **micro** 1–2 years vs. **macro** ≥ 5 years.
Trend elements: **basic needs + drivers of change → innovations** (examples, not trends).
Weak signals → cultural brailling (daily sensing) → horizon scanning (structured, STEEPLE).
Canvas: Analyse (inspirations, basic needs, drivers = shifts & triggers, emerging expectations) → Apply (innovation potential, who) → idea.
exam: Mini-case with a trend report extract: select the **drivers of change, emerging expectations and basic needs** (multiple answers).
T/F on micro vs. macro trends, primary vs. secondary data, weak signals vs. horizon scanning.
Know the four canvas fields on the Analyse side and the four innovation-potential areas on the Apply side.
traps: Innovations are **not** trends – they are examples showing that a trend exists.
Shifts are long-term macro changes, triggers are immediate – both are drivers of change.
Basic needs rarely change; if an answer describes something new, it is an expectation or a driver.
